title: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines

recommendations.text: Classify adult BP as normal, elevated, stage 1 hypertension, or stage 2 hypertension to guide prevention and treatment.
Use standardized techniques to measure and document office BP accurately when diagnosing or treating adult hypertension.
An automated oscillometric device is a reasonable choice over auscultatory measurement for adult office BP.

recommendations.section: 3.1.2. Laboratory Tests and Other Diagnostic Procedures
recommendations.text: At adult hypertension diagnosis, obtain CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lipids, glucose or HbA1c, TSH, urinalysis, urine albumin/creatinine ratio, and a 12-lead ECG to guide management.
Confirm suspected adult hypertension with ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM) or home BP monitoring (HBPM).
Use HBPM to guide antihypertensive titration, together with patient education, telehealth counseling, and clinical follow-up.
Cuffless BP devices should not be used to diagnose or manage hypertension in adults.

recommendations.section: 3.2.2. White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
recommendations.text: Before diagnosing hypertension in untreated adults with office SBP ≥130 or DBP ≥80 mm Hg, but neither SBP ≥160 nor DBP ≥100, out-of-office monitoring is reasonable to exclude white-coat hypertension.

recommendations.section: 3.2.2. White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
recommendations.text: For white-coat or masked hypertension, out-of-office monitoring is reasonable to identify progression to sustained hypertension.

recommendations.section: 3.2.2. White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
recommendations.text: In apparent resistant hypertension diagnosed by office readings, out-of-office monitoring is reasonable to exclude a white-coat effect causing pseudoresistance.

recommendations.section: 3.2.2. White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
recommendations.text: In treated adults with office SBP ≥130 or DBP ≥80 mm Hg, without resistant hypertension and without SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥100, out-of-office monitoring is reasonable to exclude white-coat effect.

recommendations.section: 3.2.2. White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
recommendations.text: In untreated adults with office BP <130/80 mm Hg, out-of-office monitoring may be considered to exclude masked hypertension.

recommendations.section: 3.2.2. White-Coat Hypertension and Masked Hypertension, and White-Coat Effect and Masked Uncontrolled Hypertension
recommendations.text: In treated adults with office BP <130/80 mm Hg, out-of-office monitoring may be considered to exclude masked uncontrolled hypertension.
Investigate specific secondary causes when clinical findings raise suspicion in an adult with hypertension.
Screen adults with resistant hypertension for primary aldosteronism even when potassium is normal.
After a positive secondary-hypertension screen, referral to a clinician with expertise in that disorder is reasonable for confirmation and treatment.

Screen for primary aldosteronism when hypertension coexists with resistance, spontaneous or diuretic-related hypokalemia, OSA, an incidental adrenal mass, family history of early hypertension, or stroke before age 40.
Primary aldosteronism screening may also be considered in stage 2 hypertension.
For an indicated primary aldosteronism screen, measure plasma aldosterone, plasma renin activity, and their ratio.
Continue most antihypertensive medications before the initial aldosteronism screen; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are the exception.
Refer to a hypertension specialist or endocrinologist after a positive aldosteronism screen or persistent suspicion from suppressed renin or disproportionate target-organ injury.
Use medical therapy for hypertension with atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis to reduce renal and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.

Referral for renal angioplasty and/or stenting is reasonable when medical therapy for atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis fails, such as resistant hypertension, worsening renal function, or acute heart failure.
Referral for renal angioplasty may be considered for hypertension due to nonatherosclerotic renal artery stenosis, including fibromuscular dysplasia.
In overweight or obese adults with hypertension and OSA, weight-loss treatment combined with CPAP can lower SBP.
CPAP can help lower BP in resistant hypertension with moderate-to-severe OSA.
For overweight or obesity, aim for ≥5% weight reduction to prevent or treat elevated BP and hypertension.
Recommend a heart-healthy dietary pattern, such as DASH, whether or not hypertension is present.
Reduce dietary sodium to <2300 mg/day, progressing toward an ideal <1500 mg/day, to prevent or treat elevated BP.

Potassium-containing salt substitutes can help prevent or treat elevated BP, particularly when home preparation or seasoning supplies most salt. In CKD or with medicines that impair potassium excretion, monitor serum potassium.

For elevated BP or hypertension, recommend moderate potassium supplementation, preferably through food. Moderate supplementation means <80 mmol (mEq)/day; CKD or medicines limiting potassium excretion require serum potassium monitoring.
Advise people who drink alcohol to aim for abstinence, or at least limit intake to ≤1 drink/day for women and ≤2 for men, to prevent or treat elevated BP.
Recommend more physical activity through structured aerobic exercise and/or resistance training to prevent or treat elevated BP.
Transcendental meditation may be considered as an adjunct to lifestyle measures or medication for BP prevention or treatment.
Other stress-management methods, including controlled breathing or yoga, may be considered as adjuncts to lifestyle measures or BP medication.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: Start BP-lowering medication in adults with hypertension when average SBP is ≥140 mm Hg to reduce cardiovascular events and mortality.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: Start BP-lowering medication in adults with hypertension when average DBP is ≥90 mm Hg to reduce cardiovascular events and mortality.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: With hypertension and established cardiovascular disease, start medication when average SBP is ≥130 mm Hg.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: With hypertension and established cardiovascular disease, start medication when average DBP is ≥80 mm Hg.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: Without clinical cardiovascular disease, start medication at average SBP ≥130 mm Hg when hypertension accompanies diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT 10-year CVD risk ≥7.5%.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: Without clinical cardiovascular disease, start medication at average DBP ≥80 mm Hg when hypertension accompanies diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT 10-year CVD risk ≥7.5%.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: Without clinical cardiovascular disease and with PREVENT 10-year CVD risk <7.5%, start medication if SBP remains ≥130 mm Hg after 3–6 months of lifestyle treatment.

recommendations.section: 5.2.2. BP Treatment Threshold and the Use of CVD Risk Estimation to Guide Drug Treatment of Hypertension
recommendations.text: Without clinical cardiovascular disease and with PREVENT 10-year CVD risk <7.5%, start medication if DBP remains ≥80 mm Hg after 3–6 months of lifestyle treatment.

recommendations.section: 5.2.3. Initial Medication Selection for Treatment of Primary Hypertension
recommendations.text: First-line antihypertensive options are thiazide-type diuretics, long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or ARBs.

recommendations.section: 5.2.4. Choice of Initial Monotherapy Versus Initial Combination Drug Therapy
recommendations.text: For stage 2 hypertension, begin two first-line agents from different classes, preferably as one combination pill, to improve control and adherence.

recommendations.section: 5.2.4. Choice of Initial Monotherapy Versus Initial Combination Drug Therapy
recommendations.text: For stage 1 hypertension, starting one first-line agent is reasonable, with dose titration and sequential addition of medications as needed.

recommendations.section: 5.2.4. Choice of Initial Monotherapy Versus Initial Combination Drug Therapy
recommendations.text: Do not combine ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and/or direct renin inhibitors with each other for hypertension because of harm.
Once-daily antihypertensive dosing improves adherence compared with multiple daily doses.
Use a single-pill combination instead of separate pills when appropriate to reduce pill burden and improve adherence.
Medication reminders, education, and self-management support can improve antihypertensive adherence.

recommendations.section: 5.2.7. BP Goal for Patients With Hypertension
recommendations.text: For confirmed hypertension with increased CVD risk, target SBP <130 mm Hg and encourage achieving <120 to reduce cardiovascular events and mortality. This table defines increased risk as PREVENT 10-year CVD risk ≥7.5%.

recommendations.section: 5.2.7. BP Goal for Patients With Hypertension
recommendations.text: For confirmed hypertension without increased CVD risk, targeting SBP <130 mm Hg and encouraging <120 may be reasonable to prevent further BP elevation.

recommendations.section: 5.2.7. BP Goal for Patients With Hypertension
recommendations.text: For confirmed hypertension with increased CVD risk, target DBP <80 mm Hg to reduce cardiovascular events and mortality.

recommendations.section: 5.2.7. BP Goal for Patients With Hypertension
recommendations.text: For confirmed hypertension without increased CVD risk, a DBP goal <80 mm Hg may be reasonable to reduce cardiovascular events.
In type 2 diabetes with hypertension, start medication at SBP ≥130 mm Hg; target <130 and encourage <120 to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
In type 2 diabetes with hypertension, start medication at DBP ≥80 mm Hg and target <80.
Thiazide-type diuretics, long-acting calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs are effective first-line BP-lowering agents in type 2 diabetes.

With diabetes and hypertension, use an ACE inhibitor or ARB when eGFR is <60 mL/min/1.73 m² or albuminuria is ≥30 mg/g; consider these agents with lesser albuminuria to slow diabetes-related kidney disease.
For hypertension with BMI ≥27 kg/m², incretin mimetics such as GLP-1 receptor agonists used for weight management may also help lower BP.
For hypertension with BMI ≥35 kg/m², bariatric surgery considered for weight loss may improve BP when combined with behavioral and antihypertensive treatment.

recommendations.section: 5.3.4. the Prevention of HF in Adults With Hypertension
recommendations.text: Treat SBP to <130 mm Hg in adults with hypertension to reduce incident heart failure.

recommendations.section: 5.3.4. the Prevention of HF in Adults With Hypertension
recommendations.text: Treat DBP to <80 mm Hg in adults with hypertension to reduce incident heart failure.

recommendations.section: 5.3.8. Hypertension Treatment in Patients With CKD
recommendations.text: With hypertension and CKD defined by eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² or albuminuria ≥30 mg/g, target SBP <130 mm Hg to reduce all-cause mortality.

recommendations.section: 5.3.8. Hypertension Treatment in Patients With CKD
recommendations.text: With hypertension, eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m², and albuminuria ≥30 mg/g, use an ACE inhibitor or ARB, but not both, to reduce CVD and slow kidney disease.
For acute spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP 150–220 mm Hg, immediate reduction to 130–<140 for at least 7 days can improve function; stop BP-lowering medication if SBP falls below 130.
When lowering BP acutely after spontaneous ICH, smooth sustained control with careful titration and avoidance of large SBP swings can improve functional outcomes.
For spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP >220 mm Hg, avoid reducing SBP below 130 because of adverse events.
Correct hypotension and hypovolemia in acute ischemic stroke to maintain systemic perfusion and organ function.
Before IV thrombolysis, lower elevated BP to <185/110 mm Hg; maintain BP below 180/105 for at least 24 hours after starting treatment.
During endovascular stroke treatment and for 24 hours afterward, maintaining BP ≤180/105 mm Hg is reasonable.
If BP is ≥220/120 mm Hg and neither IV thrombolysis nor EVT was given, with no other indication for urgent BP treatment, a 15% reduction during the first 24 hours after stroke may be reasonable.

When BP is <220/120 mm Hg after ischemic stroke without IV thrombolysis, EVT, or another urgent BP indication, starting or restarting antihypertensives within 48–72 hours does not prevent death or disability.
After successful EVT reperfusion of a large-vessel occlusion, lowering SBP below 140 mm Hg during the first 24–72 hours can worsen long-term function.
After ischemic stroke, TIA, or ICH in patients with hypertension, use a thiazide-type diuretic, ACE inhibitor, or ARB to lower BP and recurrent stroke risk.
After ischemic stroke, TIA, or ICH with hypertension, target office BP <130/80 mm Hg to reduce recurrent stroke, ICH, and other vascular events.
After ischemic stroke, TIA, or ICH without previously diagnosed hypertension, antihypertensive treatment can help when average office BP is ≥130/80 mm Hg.

recommendations.section: 5.3.9.4. Prevention of Mild Cognitive Impairment and Dementia
recommendations.text: For adults with hypertension, target SBP <130 mm Hg to prevent mild cognitive impairment and dementia.
Use team-based care to achieve sustained control in adults with uncontrolled hypertension.
Use an evidence-based plan combining HBPM and team-based care that addresses adverse social determinants of health in uncontrolled hypertension.
Integrate accurate BP measurement, timely treatment, patient engagement, and ongoing review of home readings to improve uncontrolled hypertension.
After starting or intensifying medication for uncontrolled hypertension, review adherence and response monthly until BP is controlled.
Incorporate synchronous or asynchronous health information technology into uncontrolled-hypertension care, including medication titration, to improve control, access, and adherence to care standards.
Use electronic health records and registries to identify undiagnosed or uncontrolled hypertension and direct additional care.
Telehealth interventions can help lower BP and improve office BP control in uncontrolled hypertension.
For hypertension when pregnancy is planned or established, labetalol and extended-release nifedipine are preferred agents to minimize fetal risk.
Counsel people with hypertension who plan pregnancy or become pregnant about low-dose aspirin 81 mg/day to reduce preeclampsia and its consequences.
In pregnancy, confirm SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mm Hg within 15 minutes and provide medication to reach <160/<110 within 30–60 minutes.

Treat chronic hypertension in pregnancy to <140/90 mm Hg to reduce maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. Chronic hypertension includes prepregnancy hypertension or SBP 140–159 and/or DBP 90–109 before 20 weeks.
Avoid atenolol, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors, nitroprusside, and MRAs in people planning pregnancy or who are pregnant because of fetal harm.
In resistant hypertension, reassess secondary causes, review all medications, and remove medicines that interfere with BP control when possible.
If resistant hypertension remains uncontrolled on optimal ACE inhibitor or ARB plus calcium channel blocker and thiazide-like diuretic, add an MRA when eGFR is ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m².

When an MRA is contraindicated or not tolerated in resistant hypertension, adding amiloride, a beta blocker, alpha blocker, central sympatholytic, dual endothelin-receptor antagonist, or direct vasodilator is reasonable.

Renal denervation may be considered as an adjunct in selected patients with office SBP 140–180 and DBP ≥90 mm Hg, eGFR ≥40 mL/min/1.73 m², and resistance despite optimal therapy or intolerable adverse effects from additional medications.
A multidisciplinary team experienced in resistant hypertension and renal denervation should evaluate all candidates for renal denervation.
Before renal denervation, use shared decision-making to compare BP benefits and procedural risks with continued medication and the patient's expectations.
Improve BP control in adults with hypertension to reduce the risk of orthostatic hypotension.
In adults receiving intensive BP treatment who have asymptomatic orthostatic hypotension, an SBP goal <130 mm Hg remains reasonable for cardiovascular and mortality benefit.
When starting or adding antihypertensives toward SBP <130 mm Hg, assessing symptomatic orthostatic hypotension is reasonable to detect other chronic conditions.

recommendations.section: 6.2. Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients
recommendations.text: For a hypertensive emergency with BP >180 and/or >120 mm Hg and acute target-organ injury, admit to intensive care for continuous BP/organ monitoring and consideration of parenteral treatment. This table excludes pregnancy and acute stroke.

recommendations.section: 6.2. Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients
recommendations.text: For hypertensive emergencies with a compelling condition, lower SBP to <140 mm Hg for most conditions or <120 for aortic dissection during the first hour, while monitoring other organ function.

recommendations.section: 6.2. Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients
recommendations.text: Without a compelling condition, lower SBP by no more than 25% in hour 1; if stable, reach <160/100 over the next 2–6 hours, then cautiously 130–140 over 24–48 hours.

recommendations.section: 6.2. Hypertensive Emergencies and Severe Hypertension in Nonpregnant and Nonstroke Patients
recommendations.text: For severe hypertension >180/120 mm Hg during hospitalization for a noncardiac condition without acute target-organ injury, do not use intermittent extra IV or oral antihypertensives to acutely lower BP.
Continue chronic beta blockers throughout the perioperative period in patients with hypertension undergoing major surgery.
Continuing most antihypertensives through elective major surgery is reasonable.
Holding an ACE inhibitor or ARB before major surgery may be considered to reduce intraoperative hypotension.
For elective major surgery with SBP ≥180 or DBP ≥110 mm Hg, deferral may be considered, especially in high-risk patients.
Abrupt preoperative withdrawal of a beta blocker or clonidine can cause rebound hypertension and harm.
Do not start a beta blocker on the day of surgery in a patient not already receiving one because postoperative mortality can increase.

publicationUpdates.note: Corrects comparison/grading-table presentation and aprocitentan supporting text and figure notes. The affected clinical material is not reproduced in the extracted entries.

Full primary notice reviewed: Table 16 had lithium and thiazide-type diuretics/RAS blockers in the wrong column. The correction identifies the antihypertensive drugs as thiazides/RAS blockers and lithium as the interacting drug. This drug-interaction reference table is not reproduced among the 108 formal recommendations; none requires alteration.

Table 26 corrects the interval between slow IV labetalol injections from every 2 minutes to 10-minute intervals. This dosing reference table is not reproduced among the 108 formal recommendations; none requires alteration.

coverage.note: All 108 numbered COR/LOE recommendation rows across 30 unique tables are represented once, including expert-opinion recommendations. No separately designated ungraded good-practice or consensus statements are present. Narrative supporting text, drug-dose reference tables, figures, and duplicate What Is New/Take-Home summaries are not additional recommendation rows. All three identified Hypertension correction notices were reviewed against these entries; none changes a formal recommendation row.
